headline: High-risk write and workflow overlap: ECC can modify shared developer state while ChatGPT Desktop can ingest files/screenshots, creating default-path conflict and leakage risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ChatGPT Desktop reads uploaded files, screenshots, and supported-app content, while ECC writes and manages files like ~/.claude and MCP configs. If ECC-generated content is copied into ChatGPT or surfaced through shared files, prompt-like instructions can be injected. The pathway is plausible but not proven by a documented direct bridge.
conditions: IF ECC writes attacker-controlled text into shared workspace files or prompts
IF ChatGPT Desktop ingests those files or screenshots as task context
mitigations: Separate workspaces for the two agents
Disable automatic file ingestion where possible
Review copied content before pasting into ChatGPT
Use plain-text summaries instead of raw files
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between tools

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents read files, and ChatGPT Desktop touches uploaded files, screenshots, voice, and connected-IDE code while ECC stores session summaries, hooks, and agent definitions. A shared workspace or copied artifacts could expose sensitive material from one agent to the other. The profiles do not show a guaranteed shared filesystem, so this is medium rather than high.
conditions: IF both agents access the same project directory or synced home-folder subtree
IF sensitive files are uploaded to ChatGPT Desktop after ECC has written them
mitigations: Use separate directories for each agent
Exclude secrets from shared folders
Turn off unnecessary file uploads
Rotate any exposed credentials
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ECC has shell, subprocess, filesystem write, git modification, and MCP access; ChatGPT Desktop can read files and use vendor-mediated app context plus clipboard/screen surfaces. ECC explicitly warns about separate roots to avoid overwriting session files, so concurrent writes to shared developer state are a default-path hazard if both touch the same workspace. The overlap is broad and can corrupt git or config state.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or home-directory subtree
IF ECC and ChatGPT Desktop write overlapping config, session, or git files
mitigations: Assign separate roots per agent
Pause one agent during writes by the other
Back up the workspace before concurrent runs
Restrict ECC to a dedicated branch
requires-engineering: add file locks and conflict detection

D_cascading_error.rationale: ECC’s workflow surface includes skills, hooks, and session summaries, so its outputs can become structured inputs for downstream actions. ChatGPT Desktop can consume files and app context, but the profiles do not prove it automatically acts on ECC output. That makes a verification gap plausible in default workflows, though not enough for high severity.
conditions: IF ECC-generated summaries or findings are fed into ChatGPT Desktop without human review
IF ChatGPT Desktop is then used to draft or execute follow-on actions from those summaries
mitigations: Require human review before reuse
Convert outputs into checked templates
Cross-check claims against source files
Limit ECC outputs to summaries only
requires-engineering: add verification gates between agents

E_compliance.rationale: ECC explicitly handles retention, context, and agent-data settings, while ChatGPT Desktop touches uploaded files, screenshots, voice, and connected-IDE code. If regulated data is placed into both systems, differing retention or residency controls could create a compliance mismatch. The profiles do not specify a concrete jurisdictional conflict, so medium is the highest supportable severity.
conditions: IF regulated data is processed by both agents
IF their retention or residency settings differ for the same data class
mitigations: Classify data before use
Keep regulated data out of one agent
Align retention settings
Document residency assumptions
requires-engineering: formalize a data-processing agreement
